# Problem Set 2 : Probability and Uncertainty

# Problem 1: Simulation
```{r}

# Make the simulation reproducible
set.seed(123)

# Sample size
n <- 1000

# Generate the confounder
Zi <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Generate treatment, which depends on the confounder
Xi <- 0.5 * Zi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Generate the outcome
Yi <- 2 + 3 * Xi + 1.5 * Zi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Create the dataset
simulation_data <- data.frame(Yi, Xi, Zi)

# Fit the true model and print the summary
model_true <- lm(Yi ~ Xi + Zi, data = simulation_data)
summary(model_true)

```

# 1-(a) 
# demonstrate that the coefficient for your treatment variable follows the central limit theorem.
# demonstrate that the coefficient's sampling distribution is approximately normal.
# if we repeatedly drew new samples and estimated the treatment effect, what would the estimates look like?
```{r}

## Set up the simulation
set.seed(123)

n <- 1000
simulations <- 5000

## Create a vector containing 5000 zeros.
beta_Xi <- numeric(simulations)

## Starts a loop = repeat the data generation and estimation
for (s in seq_len(simulations)) {
  
  # Generate a new dataset in each simulation
  Zi <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  Xi <- 0.5 * Zi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  Yi <- 2 + 3 * Xi + 1.5 * Zi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  
  # Fit the correctly specified model = Estimate the true model in each sample
  model <- lm(Yi ~ Xi + Zi)
  
  # Save the estimated coefficient on Xi = Save the treatment coefficient
  beta_Xi[s] <- coef(model)["Xi"]
}

#Summarize the sampling distribution
mean(beta_Xi)
sd(beta_Xi)

## Display two plots side by side (historgram on the left & Q-Q plot on the right)
# divide the plotting area into one row and two columns
par(mfrow = c (1, 2))

# Histogram with a fitted normal density
hist(beta_Xi,
     breaks = 40,
     probability = TRUE,
     main = "Sampling Distribution of the Xi Coefficient",
     xlab = "Estimated coefficient on Xi",
     col = "lightblue",
     border = "white")

# Add a normal curve for comparison
curve(dnorm(x, mean(beta_Xi), sd = sd(beta_Xi)),
     add = TRUE,
     col = "red",
     lwd = 2)
     

# Mark the true treatment effect
abline(v = 3, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2, lty = 2) #lwd: twice the default thickness, #lty = 2: specifies a dashed line



# Additional Check: Normal Q-Q plot
qqnorm(beta_Xi, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot") #qqnorm: draw the comparison points
qqline(beta_Xi, col = "red", lwd = 2) #qqline: adds a reference line
# If the estimates are approximately normally distributed, the points lie roughly along the red line.


```

# 1-(b) 
# using one dataset, estimate how much the treatment coefficient would vary across samples by using the bootstrap.
## a smaller standard error = more precise estimate.
# using one dataset and repeatedly resample its observation.

```{r}

# Make the simulation reproducible
set.seed(123)

# Sample size
n <- 1000

# Generate the confounder
Zi <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Generate treatment, which depends on the confounder
Xi <- 0.5 * Zi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Generate the outcome
Yi <- 2 + 3 * Xi + 1.5 * Zi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Create the dataset
simulation_data <- data.frame(Yi, Xi, Zi)


set.seed(456)

## Number of bootstrap repetitions
B <- 5000

## Number of observations in the original dataset
n <- nrow(simulation_data)

## Storage for the bootstrap treatment coefficients
boot_beta_Xi <- numeric(B)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  
  # Randomly select n row numbers with replacement
  sampled_rows <- sample(seq_len(n), size = n, replace = TRUE)

  # Create a bootstrap dataset using those rows
  boot_data <- simulation_data[sampled_rows, ]
  
  # Estimate the same model using the bootstrap dataset
  boot_model <- lm(Yi ~ Xi + Zi, data = boot_data)
  
  # Save the estimated treatment coefficient
  boot_beta_Xi[b] <- coef(boot_model) ["Xi"]
}

## Bootstrapped standard error
bootstrap_se <- sd(boot_beta_Xi)
bootstrap_se

```
# Answer: the bootstrapped standard error for the coefficient of the treatment variable is 0.030.

# 1-(c) 
# fit a model that omits the confounding variable (Zi)
# repeat the (a) with the new model omitting confounding variable and create the plot
# compare the correct model and omitted variable model
```{r}

set.seed(123)

n <- 1000
simulations <- 5000

## Store treatment estimates from both models
beta_correct <- numeric(simulations)
beta_omitted <- numeric(simulations)

for (s in seq_len(simulations)) {
  
  # Generate data using the true model
  Zi <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  Xi <- 0.5 * Zi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  Yi <- 2 + 3 * Xi + 1.5 * Zi + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd =1)
  
  # Correct model: includes the confounder
  model_correct <- lm(Yi ~ Xi + Zi)
  # New model: omits the confounder
  model_omitted <- lm (Yi ~ Xi)
  
  # Save the treatment coefficients
  beta_correct[s] <- coef(model_correct)["Xi"]
  beta_omitted[s] <- coef(model_omitted)["Xi"]
}

## Compare the centers, standard deviations, and biases
data.frame(
  Model = c("Includes Zi", "Omits Zi"),
  Mean = c(mean(beta_correct), mean(beta_omitted)),
  SD = c(sd(beta_correct), sd(beta_omitted)),
  Bias = c(mean(beta_correct) - 3, mean(beta_omitted) - 3)
)

## Set a common horizontal axis for comparison
plot_limits <- range(c(beta_correct, beta_omitted, 3))

## Display two plots side by side
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))


## Left plot: Correct model's sampling distribution = histogram of correct model
hist(beta_correct,
     breaks = 40,
     probability = TRUE,
     xlim = plot_limits,
     main = "Model Including Zi",
     xlab = "Estimated coefficient on Xi",
     col = "lightblue",
     border = "white")

curve(dnorm(x,
            mean = mean(beta_correct),
            sd = sd(beta_correct)),
      add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

abline(v = 3, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2, lty = 2)


## Right plot: Omitted-confounder model's sampling distribution = histogram of omitted model
hist(beta_omitted,
     breaks = 40,
     probability = TRUE,
     xlim = plot_limits,
     main = "Model Omitting Zi",
     xlab = "Estimated coefficient on Xi",
     col = "lightpink",
     border = "white")

curve(dnorm(x,
            mean = mean(beta_omitted),
            sd = sd(beta_omitted)),
      add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

abline(v = 3, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2, lty = 2)


```
# Answer: Both sampling distributions are approximately normal, however omitting the confounder shifts the center from the true effect of 3 to 3.6, presenting that normality does not ensure valid statistical tests of the causal treatment effect.

# Problem 2: Data Analysis

# 2-(a)
# conduct a hypothesis test for a difference in means. 
# decide what are the hypotheses are, whether to use a t-test or a z-test and the level of significance
# compare the average outcome of two groups & assess whether the observed difference = a difference in population means
# Average outcome of treatment group - Average outcome of control group


# Do students who receive tutoring have different average scores from students who do not?
```{r}

# Enter the hypothetical exam scores
tutoring <- c(78, 85, 88, 90, 76, 84, 92, 81, 87, 89)
no_tutoring <- c(72, 75, 80, 77, 69, 74, 82, 78, 73, 76)

# Calculate group means
mean(tutoring)
mean(no_tutoring)

# Calculate the difference: tutoring - no tutoring
mean(tutoring) - mean(no_tutoring)

# Conduct a two-sided Welch independent-samples t-test
test_result <- t.test(
  x = tutoring,
  y = no_tutoring,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  mu = 0, # specifies that hypothesized difference is zero
  var.equal = FALSE, # selects Welch's t-test
  conf.level = 0.95
)

# Display the results
test_result

```
# Answer:
# Using hypothetical exam scores for 10 tutored and 10 non-tutored students, I tested whether the two groups have different population mean scores. The hypotheses were: 

Ho : mu(tutoring) - mu(no_tutoring) equals 0.
HA : mu(tutoring) - mu(no_tutoring) does not equal to 0.

# I used a two-sided Welch two-sample t-test because the groups contain different students, the population standard deviations are unknown, and equal population variances are not assumed. The two-sided alternative enables a difference in either direction. I selected confidence level of 0.05. The test assumes independent observations and approximately normal population score distributions, particularly given the small samples. 

# The tutoring group's mean was 85.0, compared with 75.6 for the no_tutoring group, a difference of 9.4 points. The test yielded t = 4.5484, df = 16.507, and p = 0.0003053. Since the p-value is below 0.05, I reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is statistically significant evidence of a difference in population means. The 95% confidence interval for the difference is [5.03, 13.77] points.

# Substantively, the tutoring group scored 9.4 points higher on average, a potentially meaningful difference on a 100-point exam. However, this comparison does not establish that tutoring caused higher scores because random assignment to tutoring was not specified.


# standard errors: measure unit for uncertainty in the estimated difference
# t-value: how much or many times your standard errors are away from zero
# p-value: how unusual your results would be if the null hypothesis were true
# null hypothesis : the claim you test against the data - which often has no difference (significance) and no association.
# Rejecting the null hypothesis = your data provided enough evidence against the claim being tested = two groups have equal population mean exam scores

# 2-(b)
# use the same data, fit the linear model.
# interpret the coefficient, standard error, t-value, and p-value.
```{r}

# Same data from (a)
tutoring <- c(78, 85, 88, 90, 76, 84, 92, 81, 87, 89)
no_tutoring <- c(72, 75, 80, 77, 69, 74, 82, 78, 73, 76)

# Combine the scores and create the group indicator
exam_data <- data.frame(
  score = c(tutoring, no_tutoring),
  tutoring = c(rep(1, 10), rep(0, 10))
)

# Fit the linear model
model <- lm(score ~ tutoring, data = exam_data)

# Display the regression results
summary(model)

```

# Answer:
# I fitted the linear model, where tutoring equals 1 for tutored students and 0 for non-tutored students. The intercept of 75.6 represents the mean score for non-tutored students. The tutoring coefficient of 9.4 indicates that tutored students scored 9.4 points higher on average. Its standard error of 2.067 measures the estimated sampling uncertainty of this difference. The t-value of 4.548 means the coefficient is 4.548 standard errors above the hypothesized value of zero. The p-value of 0.000249 is below the confidence level of 0.05, so I reject the null hypothesis that the tutoring coefficient equals to zero. Thus, tutoring status is statistically significantly associated with exam scores, although this does not establish causation without random assignment.

# standard error = measures unit for uncertainty in the estimated difference.
# t-value = how many times the standard errors are far from zero.
# p-value = how unusual your results would be if the null hypothesis were true.
# null hypothesis = the claim you test against the data - often which there is no difference (significance) and no association.
# rejecting the null hypothesis = your estimate is significant enough

# 2-(c)
# conduct a permutation test for my hypothesis
# plot the null distribution and mark the observed estimates on the plot
# discuss the results: compare the permutation p-values with the p-values from 2-(a) and 2-(b).

# Permutation test = checks whether your observed group difference is unusually large by repeatedly shuffling the group labels = is the difference compatible with ordinary variation under the null hypothesis, or is it surpisingly large? 

```{r}

## Same data from (a)
tutoring <- c(78, 85, 88, 90, 76, 84, 92, 81, 87, 89)
no_tutoring <- c(72, 75, 80, 77, 69, 74, 82, 78, 73, 76)

## Combine the scores and create the group indicator
exam_data <- data.frame(
  score = c(tutoring, no_tutoring),
  tutoring = c(rep(1, 10), rep(0, 10))
)

# =======================================================================================================

## make the random shuffling reproducible
set.seed(123)

## calculate the observed difference in means
observed_difference <- with(
  exam_data, 
  mean(score[tutoring == 1]) - mean(score[tutoring == 0])
)

## number of permutations (choose 10,000 shuffles + create 10,000 storage positions to store their results)
B <- 10000
## store the difference from each permutation
permuted_differences <- numeric(B)


## shuffle the labels and recalculate the difference
for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  
  # shuffle the group labels without replacement (Not allowed: the same card twice within a single shuffle)
  shuffled_labels <- sample(exam_data$tutoring)
  
  # calculate the difference using the shuffled labels 
  permuted_differences[b] <-
    mean(exam_data$score[shuffled_labels == 1]) - 
    mean(exam_data$score[shuffled_labels == 0])
}

## Calculate the permutation p-value
## Two-sided permutation p-value
## add 1 to the numerator and denominator for Monte Carlo sampling
permutation_p <- (
  sum(abs(permuted_differences) >= abs(observed_difference)) + 1
) / (B + 1)

# print the observed difference annd permutation p-value
observed_difference
permutation_p

# =============================================================================================================

## Plot the null differences = Plot the shuffled differences
hist(permuted_differences,
     breaks = 40, 
     main = "Permutation Null Distribution",
     xlab = "Difference in mean scores (points)",
     col = "lightblue",
     border = "white",
     xlim = range(c(permuted_differences,
                    -abs(observed_difference),
                    abs(observed_difference))))

## Mark the observed statistic = mark the actual result
abline(v = observed_difference,
       col = "red", lwd = 2)

## Mark the equally extreme difference in the opposite direction = mark the opposite-tail cutoff
abline(v = -abs(observed_difference),
       col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)


# permutation p-value counts results at / beyond these two lines
legend("topright",
       legend = c("Observed difference: + 9.4",
                  "Opposite-tail cutoff: -9.4"),
       col = "red",
       lty = c(1, 2),
       lwd = 2, 
       bty = "n")


```

```{r}

## Compare p-values from all three p-values
c(
  Welch_t_test = t.test(
    score ~ tutoring, data = exam_data)$p.value,
  
  Linear_model = summary(
    lm(score ~ tutoring, data = exam_data))$coefficients["tutoring", "Pr(>|t|)"],
  
  Permutation_test = permutation_p
)

```

# Answer: I conducted a two-sided permutation test using the difference in mean exam scores as the test statistic. I shuffled the tutoring labels 10,000, while preserving the 10 students in each group. The plotted null distribution is centered near zero, whereas the observed difference of 9.4 points lies far in the right tail. The permutation p-value is approximately 0.000600, which is smaller than the confidence level of 0.05, so I reject the null hypothesis. 

# In terms of comparing the three p-values, the permutation p-value seems slightly larger than the p-values from Welch's t-test (0.000305) and the linear model (0.000249). However, all three methods provide strong evidence against equal population means. The numerical difference reflect their different methods and assumptions, along with Monte Carlo variation in the permutation estimate. Overall, the tutored students scored higher on average, although these results alone do not establish causation.
